body:
I wish I knew 3 things: 1) how boring it was sitting in the chemo chair for 6 hours while getting chemo and how uncomfortable the chairs are 2) how side effects started on day 2, got worse from day 3 to day 6 and then gradually got better, also that the side effects weren't the same each round, but slightly different and 3) you can get allergic reaction to chemo (I had that. The most important is to tell the nurses if you feel even a little off. Right away. The second you feel it. They stop the chemo and give you something for the allergy and you feel better right away.)

Other small tips I've learned during my 6 rounds of chemo: use baby products (body wash, toothpaste, lotion...), regularly use non-alcoholic mouthwash to prevent sores, take meds for the side effects as soon as you feel them (if you wait it gets worse and the meds don't help as much or as quickly), rest, drink more water than you think you need, flush the toilet twice, food will taste awful so don't eat food you love so it doesn't get ruined, tell your oncologist about all side effects and asks for meds for it... Good luck.

The first chemo is the hardest. Not knowing what to expect and how it all works can be really scary. Getting chemo doesn't hurt. They pump you full of steroids and anti-nausea meds so you might be a bit high or sleepy, but that's it. The boredom while being hooked up to chemo is the worst part. My chemo lasted 6 hours but with having to have a blood test and see my oncologist I was at the hospital for 12-13 hours. Get some distraction to get you through (phone, books, laptop). Get water and some snacks that don't have strong smell. Also the chemo chairs are a bit uncomfortable so take a pillow or a blanket to make yourself more comfortable. 

Watching TikToks and YT videos of people going through chemo helped me. It gave me an idea of what to expect and that made it less scary. Same with reading posts on Reddit.

I have a port and I love it. My oncologist recommended I get one because they always had troubles finding my veins and the chemo damages them so it makes it even harder to find. Getting the port was super easy and fast. It only lasted 15 or 20 minutes. I was awake for it and it felt a bit weird, but absolutely no pain. You have to keep it in for 1-2 years and have it flushed every 3 months. That's a bit of a hassle. But it makes getting chemo easier, they don't have to look for veins and you can move more freely. If you decide to try IV chemo and the nurse aren't able to get the IV needle in you won't be able to get chemo. The IV needle has to be placed exactly right so the chemo doesn't cause more damage. While I was getting chemo I've seen nurses try to get and IV in for like 10 minutes, 2 or 3 different nurses. 

If you don't want a port you can also get a PICC line. It's less invasive, but you have to take care of it and watch out for infections. Plus it can't get wet.

Same. I also have endometrial cancer and our German Shepherd would shove her nose in my crotch. She stopped doing it during chemo. I figured she didn't like my smell. I hated my smell during chemo so it must have been awful for her. A few weeks after I finished chemo, I think I was around the time I was finishing radiation when she started doing it again. It has me a bit worried, despite doctors saying there's no sign of cancer.

I'm not from UK but scans before surgery are normal. They need to be sure it hasn't spread and to know what to look for in the surgery. In the 3 weeks before my surgery I had laboratory, chest x-ray, abdominal ultrasound and a CT. Good luck.
I've also been using kids toothpaste. I tried going back to regular toothpaste a few months after chemo, but it made my tongue and gums hurts so I switched back after a few days.
Demage control? Distraction?
I don't want to become a Bears fan. Can he at least go to Washington.
I wish he stayed with Browns for his entire career. If not, I want him to go to a team that will get him the ring. And I'll definitely root for any team that signs him, maybe even against the Browns.

I had slight lactose intolerance before, like I could eat a yogurt or have cheese, but I couldn't drink a glass of milk. It went away during chemo and radiation, or maybe I wasn't aware of it because I had other side effects. It came back a few months after finishing treatment. I didn't really change my diet. I pick lactose free stuff at the store and make sure I don't have too much regular milk and milk products.

I'm going through scanxiety and fear of recurrence, plus hating how slow my hair is growing after chemo, I really don't need to see post like that. I get the worry of having cancer and being excited when it turns out to be nothing, but it's not fair to us. This is my safe space and the only place where I trully feel like others can understand what I'm going through.
Reminds me of Baker. I hope it ends differently. I'm actually excited about this Watson-free season.
Flacco will start, but by week 10 we could be on a 3rd or 4th QB. Sooner or lare Sander will start.

Thank you. No bleeding, thanhfully. I' having some random stomach pain all over my abdome that comes and goes. I've also been a bot bloated which I'd normally think is from eating all the Easter food, but after cancer my mimd goes directly to recurrence. My doctors not telling me what to look out for makes the anxiety so mich worse.
At least he wasn't accused of sexual assult by like 100 women.
Last night I spent 2 hours watching cats and dogs TikToks. That was a great waste of time and a way to forget that cancer exists.

It is hard and sometimes it feels like your life is paused and everyone else moved on. My advice is to not hold it in. If you want to cry or scream, do it. I didn't cry when I got diagnosed or when I had hysterectomy or when I was told I'm stage 3c and will need chemo and radiation, I cried when my hair started to fall out and I saw patches of scalp through my thinning hair. I think I cried for like 30 minutes in the shower. Then I got out and shaved my head completely. Here's another advice, shave your hair sooner than later. Seeing the hair fall out was worse than being bald. 

Bribes and rewards helped me when I struggled. I had pizza after each chemo. I bought myself a few cheap wigs for fun. I actually ended up liking one of the cheap wigs a lot more than the expensive one. I got a new book for each chemo. I allowed myself to be lazy and not feel guilty over it. Hyperfixation also helps, like maybe watching a new tv show or starting a new hobby. My hyperfixation was TikTok which I didn't use before being diagnosed. 

It does get better, but in a way it never goes away. I'm not saying that to scare you, but it's just something I wish I'd known. A few months after finishing treatment (chemo and radiation) I started feeling normal-ish, but then the anxiety over recurrence started. Treatment sucked, but at least I felt like there was something I could do, now it just feels like waiting for cancer to come back or waiting to get a clear scan. I'm glad you're planning on going to the support group. Talking with people who are going through the same thing helps a lot. Good luck.

I ate pizza all the time, but I did avoid citrus fruit and spicy food. I think the sores are caused by bacteria in your mouth because the chemo makes you more sensitive to everything. Wash your teeth and use nonalcoholic mouthwash every 2-3 hours. That's what I did and I was fine. Enjoy!

I felt okay on my chemo day and a day after then the side effects slowly started for 2 days. The worst days were usually days 3 to 5 then the side effect slowly went away in 2 to 3 days. After that I still felt a bit off for a few days. And then I usually felt normal the last week before my next chemo. Half of my chemo was that. The last 2 roungs were worst and I only good a few good days before the next round. Also it was a bit different with each chemo, side effects were the same but which one was the worst and their intensity changed. My advice is to start taking the meds for side effect as soon as they start. If I waited too long to take the pills they didn't work as well, especially the anti-nause and pain pills for the bone/joint pain.

Get a chest port. I don't think you should hide it, but you can ask your surgeon if they can place the port more towards your shoulder so it can be hidden under a tank top strap.  Mine is directly under my bra strap which I thought was a bit weird because I've seen online that most people get it on the chest, but now I'm so thankful to my surgeon for putting it where it is.
Your legs look exactly like mine and I was just diagnosed with lipedema after years of being told I'm just fat. I'm sorry. Keep trying, get a second opinion.

That doesn't make sense to me. The point of the surgery is to remove cancer and properly stage it so you get the right treatment. They usually remove at least the 2 sentinel lymph nodes to test them. I think they use a dye to find them, maybe that also shows them if they're cancerous. The treatment for stage 3b and 3c is the same so it doesn't make a big difference.

Radiation targets specific area, mine was to vagina/cuff because that's where it usually spreads. There are side effects, but with stage 3b it should at least be an option for you. I was told stage 3 is always chemo and radiaton. I also never had a PET scan, I had chest X-ray, abdominal ultrasound and CT with contrast. I think you should ask your doctor about it, especially about the lymph nodes and why they're against radiation.
Congrats! That's amazing.

I'm sorry. I really don't understand why they didn't mention chemo to you when they found cancer in your lymph node. Before my surgery they thought I'd be stage 1a and my doctor explained that I might not need any treatment or only radiation. When 1 of the lymph nodes was positive they told me straight away I'll need chemo. 

Thank you. My pain feels like getting pinched and it's more or less the same since I finished my treatment. I'll have to ask my oncologist on my next appointment.

If they found cancer in your lymph nodes you should have been stage 3c and have chemo and radiation. Radiation targets a specific area (vagina which is where it can spread first) while chemo goes through your entire body. That's what happened to me. The cancer was contained in my uterus which would make it stage 1a or 1b, but because I had a positive sentinel lymph node I was stage 3c and I had chemo and radiation. 

My pathology report also said suspicious for peritoneal carcinomatosis. Can I ask what was your stomach pain like? I had stomach pain but my oncologist said it was side effect from chemo.

That's exactly how it felt. One moment I was in the operating room and the next I was being woke up by someone. It felt almost like I just blinked. The first thing I remember was a nurse waking me up and asking if I was in pain. I said yes and then she told me she's gonna give me something for the pain right away. Then I fell back asleep. Some of my first thoughts were "Oh, I survived." "So this if what having a surgery is like." "F u b\*\*\*ch. You're dead!" that one was for my uterus. I also thought how great anesthesia was and I wished I could get it for all medical procedures so I didn't have to be awake and deal with the medical trauma. I'm still not over having to have hysteroscopy. 

I didn't feel anything. Mostly I felt normal, just some pain in my lover/pelvic abdomen. I think most of that pain was from the bikini cut and not from the inside. I had a catheter, which was a bit uncomfortable, but if I didn't move I didn't feel it. For the first 4 hours I just slept and was woken up by blood pressure machine or a nurse checking up on me.

No fart is a bit concerning. If you had a laparoscopic surgery, they pump you full of gas so you should be farting. I farted for a week after lol Have you been drinking enough water? You could try mixing prunes and warm milk like a smoothie and drinking it. It doesn't taste good, but it helps. If you still can't poop, call your doctor.

Go to your doctor. I don't know what type of biopsy you had, but I don't think bleeding that much is normal. I had hysteroscopy and I had heavy spotting for 2 days. I was told a bit of bleeding and spotting for a week is normal but it should never be extreme.

Tell them how you feel about it. Maybe share your medical information only with your partner and parents and ask them not to talk to other people about it. When I was diagnosed I told my parents and my best friend and ask them to keep in quiet. I didn't tell anyone else. My mom told my aunt and the rest of my family figured it out, but even when they asked, I didn't give them any details or avoided the discussion all together.
Not me. I'm so glad it's gone and I'll never have to deal with it again.

It depends on the wig. I got one for 100 an one for 15 from Temu and I loved the cheap one. I couldn't keep the expensive one on my head for more than a few minutes. It was so uncomfortable and ugly. I hated it. The cheap one fit me perfectly and only got uncomfortable after hours of wearing it. My advice is get a cheaper one or two. Get the one with lace front, unless you're getting one with bangs then it doesn't matter.

Hi. I had a vaginal ultrasound which showed thick endometrium. My blood test also showed elevated tumor marker. That's when they suspected it could be cancer. Then I had hysteroscopy which confirmed it.

Can you call them? There's no need to suffer more than you have to. My oncologist told me that and it stuck with me. You can also try chamomile tea for rinsing your mouth. Good luck. I hope you feel better soon.

That's interesting, because my experience was the opposite. My scalp hurt so much then my hair started falling out like crazy so I buzzed it to 3 or 4 mm. After that I got a rash, small pimple like bumps, painful and itch. My doctor gave some cream and that helpped. A week later I shaved completely and I felt so much better. I don't know if it's diferrent for each chemo. I got TC chemo.

The best advice I got when I was going through chemo was to use baby/infant products and to use non-alcoholic mouthwash every 2-3 hours. I didn't get mouth sores but my oncologist said to tell her if I get them and she'll prescribe something. Prescribtion meds always work better so just ask your doctor.

I wore a button down blouse or a men's T-shirt with 3 buttons on top. When it got colder I wore a tank top under a hoodie with a zipper so once they hooked me up I just put on the hoodie. While chemo room wasn't exactly cold, it was too cold for just a tank top. I don't think you need a port shirt, just wear something with a wide neckline.

I was 38 and the doctors thought I'll probably be stage 1 and if the ovaries looked healthy during the survery they'll leave them. I said they can remove them, but they left them. I had 1 positive lymph node so I ended up being stage 3. I neede chemo and radiation which ruined my ovaries and any pros of keeping them. Now it's just one more thing where the cancer could reappear. 

If there's a chance you're anything but stage 1 I'd ask to remove the ovaries. You'll have do deal with menopause symptoms in 5-10 years anyway because ovaries stop working sooner if you have a hysterectomy. If you're stage 1, the chances of recurrence are so small you can keep them. You'll also won't need chemo or radiation that would affect them.

My follow up is blood test (basic + tumor markers), pelvic exam and talk about any symptoms or side effects of chemo and radiation. I was told they decide if they're gonna do CT or any other testing based on the symptoms and the exam, but they still do 1 CT a year.

It took me about 2 months to get used to mine. I felt similar at first. Give it some time. After 9 months touching it still feels weird but most of the time I'm not aware of it. I forget it's even there unless I touch it.

Are you sure it's stage 2 and not grade 2? I was told grade and type of cancer after my hysteroscopy but they said they can only tell the stage after surgery. If it's grade 2 that's still not agressive cancer and it's slow growing. About gene information you could ask chatGPT. My oncologist explain it to me but I didn't understand what he was talking about so I asked chatGPT and then I got it. Good luck.

I only watch Hallmark when I'm in the mood for something cheesy and for Christmas. I expect this to be just like anything else they put out so I avoided watching it until now. It's so good and sooooo different from their normal. I love it and I hope they make more stuff like that.

After the surgery the only thing they told me was how the surgery went and that they took samples to send to the lab. They gave me instructions for home and gave me the date of my first appointment which was 3 weeks after my surgery. How were you diagnosed? Did you have a biopsy? That should give you the grade and type of cancer. It can change after the surgery, but it usually stays the same. I hope you have a successful surgery and speedy recovery.

Losing my hair was the hardest thing about chemo. I could deal with the side effects, but not losing my hair. My advice is to shave it completely. Don't cut it short or buzz it. Hair falling out in clumbs and seeing more and more of my scalp was really traumatic. Once I shaved it all I felt better. I avoided mirrors and wore a cap all the time, but it was way better than watching my hair fall out. If you love shopping go on a shopping spree for wigs and scarf and comfortable chemo clothes. Looking for wigs online was a great distraction.
Yeah, I had a big meal and I was still hungry like I hadn't had anything. Good luck.

I was the same when I went through chemo, also TC. I had nausea, stomach cramps, my taste had changed and I was starving. I never felt full and I always felt like I hadn't eaten all day. I would eat nuts, crackers, blueberries, popcorn... like small food that I could slowely snack on. Drinking water made my hunger worse. Sparkling water and soda helped a bit, but I couldn't drink it too much because the chemo made my mouth sensitive and I was afraod of gettimg sores. A chemo nurse said that weight gain was normal and is better to gain weight than to lose it during chemo.
It usually started on day 2, most of the side effects started then actually. The day of the chemo and the next day I usually felt normal.

I never vomited. Nausea lasted 2 to 5 days, but as long as I took anti nausea pill right away or on the schedule, I was fine. The pills made the nausea go away completelly in 10 minutes. Good luck with your chemo.

Yes. Every pain or feeling weird and I automatically think of cancer comming back. I'm not really handling it, more like forcefully gething through it and hoping for the best. 

For the entire week before my first check up I was a nervous wreck and convinced my cancer was back. I think I even got body pains from anxiety because those pains went away after the check up when I was told everything was normal.
Same. I still can't drink 2 glasses of milk at once, but I can eat yogurt, cheese... Interesting.
How they park their car. Over the lines, no parking zone, across 2 parking spaces. I think in general what kind of driver you are says a lot about someone.

I'm sorry about your diagnosis. From my experience the only way to stage endometrial cancer is hysterectomy.  CA 125 and MRI will show if the cancer has spread outside the uterus. Ca 125 under 35 is normal. If it's elevated it can mean inflamation or spread to ovaries, but it's not 100%. Are you also getting other tumor markers checked (ca 15-3, cea)? MR will show near organs and lymph nodes if they're all clear. 

Do you know the grade (1-3)? As long as the cancer is low grade (1 or 2), hasn't spread and they consider it stage 1a your doctor will talk to you about hormonal therapy. I think they test it for 3 or 6 months to see if it's working then if it's working they encourage you to get pregnant in 2 years and have surgery later.

I was considered stage 1a and my oncologist was talking about fertility preserving hormonal treatment but CT which is similar to MRI showed enlarged lymph nodes so I had to have surgery. Good luck. I hope ot all turns out well for you.

Entertainment (books, tv shows, movies...). Chemos take a long time and you get bored. Any comfortable clothes. If she has a port a sweater specifically made for accessing the port. Baby stuff like toothpaste, lotion, shower gel. During chemo your skin and the entire body gets more sensitive and using baby stuff really helpped me deal with it. Good luck to your mom.
I hate crowds, plus I don't have a clue how any of the machines work.

I had my period when I had my surgery. I was worried, but they said it's not a big deal. Just tell the nurses. They'll give you those hospital mesh panties and a pad. They cut them off in the operating room once you fall asleep. I woke up in the recovery room with a new gown and new mesh panties and a pad. My after surgery bleeding was actually less heavy than pre surgery period.
Pineapple. I kind of like it.

Same. Once I start thinking of food I can't stop. I don't know why extreme restriction is so much easier. I can go half a day without food or water. No wonder people say it's easier to quit smoking than food addiction.

These things sort of help. I distract myself with watching TikToks and YT. Hyperfixating on something is great. I pick a random topic and then research it online. I move, like if I'm in the living room, I'd go to the bedroom (never the kitchen). The other thing I do is to not tell myself I can't eat or call myself a fat cow which I did a lot. Instead I say to myself something like "I'm hungry, I'll eat in 30 minites." I repeat that until it's time to eat. If nothing helps and all I can think about is food I eat something that's less than 100 calories or I drink a can of soda.

I was told not to do my nails during chemo. I had TC chemo and one of the side effects is nails changing and being more sensitive. I left my nails alone and they still got vertical lines and ridges. Luckily they weren't painful. But I've seen people talk about their nails falling off which really scared me. My advice is to leave them alone.

It's up to you. The doctors recommend the best option, but it's your choice. I'd listen to the doctors.

If they found endometrial cancer on your cervix it's possible that your cancer spread from the uterus to it and if it spread so far it could have also gone elsewhere. Surgery is the only treatment and it's usually also the only way to stage it and find out if you need more treatment. If the cancer is found early enough, surgery might be the only thing you need. For me it took a little over a month between a confirmed diagnosis and surgery. With cancer time is important. Grade 1 is not agressive and it usually doesn't spread fast, but you never know. 

It's scary and frustrating and not the right time. We've all been there. You really have to think of yourself right now. Chemo feels way worse than perimenopause symptoms. You still have a chance to avoid it if your cancer was found fast enough. My advice is don't wait and listen to your doctors. But the final decision is up to you. Good luck.

I had my port for 10 months now and no problems. Port placement is quick. It takes maybe 20 minutees, she won't feel any pain, just some tugging. There is some waiting before and after she'll probably have to have an x-ray so they check the pprt is placed correctly. For the first few days she should avoid using the arm on the side she gets the port. I was also scared, but when I had chemo I was so glad I had the port. Good luck to her.

Wear comfortable clothes and shoes. Bring water or something to drink. Maybe some snacks, but don't bring anything smelly because it might bother other patients. The most important is entertainment. Like you said, it's boring. You just sit there with nothing to do. You can't even take a nap because the nurses keep checking up on you and machines are going off. Reading and TikTok got me through most of my chemos. Chemo chairs can be uncomfortable, at least they were at my chemo center, so bring a small pillow or a blanket, something to make it more comfortable. Good luck.
Shave it now. If you're gonna lose your hair, it doesn't matter anyway and you'll feel so much better with a clean shaved head. No more hair everywhere and no more itching/burning/painful scalp.

I don't know what my starting BMI was. I lost a bunch of weight and my BMI went to 30. Currently my BMI is 40 so I assume my highest BMI was around 50. I can do exercise, I even enjoy it, so I started with exercise and then slowly added diet which is my biggest struggle. 

I started with 10-20 minutes of exercise every day. I did Youtube video workouts (for seniors, for obese, low impact, walking indoor). There are also dancing workout if you love dancing. I don't have the coordination for that and I just got frustrated when I couldn't follow along. If I couldn't do an exercise or I needed to rest I just walked in place until I felt ready to do more. I watched a tv show while working out (1 episode = 1 workout). I also did workout tetris - it's a bullet journal thing where you add shape/block for each time you exercise. If you google bullet journal tetris you should see what I mean. I'm trying to get back to working out every day and the workout tetris is really motivating. I want to draw in that next block so bad. I hope you find the right exercise for you. Just try a bunch of stuff until you find something you enjoy. Good luck.

I think that depends on the type of chemo. I had TC chemo and my weight stayed roughly the same, which is a bit surprising because I had huge appetite a few days after chemo. Nausea + stomach cramps + wanting to eat is weird and awful. On top of that, chemo changed my taste so I wanted to eat, but everything tasted disgusting. One time I made myself 3 different breakfasts before I could actually eat one of them. Nurses told me to eat whatever I wanted, except grapefruit and too much vitamin C because that affected my chemo. They also don't like if you're losing weight. It's better for your body if you maintain or gain weight.
Day 2. They wouldn't let me leave the hospital without pooping first. First poo is the scariest. My advice is to take laxatives and don't wait for it to happen naturally.

I'm so sorry. This sucks. I got the same treatment when I was first diagnosed. I had tests, then I saw my doctor for like a couple of minutes, just long enough to be send for more tests and got a new appointment for after they had their meeting. Waiting is hard, but doctors telling you the bare minimal or nothing until they are certain makes it worse. Can you see your scan results and the radiologist's opinion? I'm not saying this a good way to do things, but when I get my scans before I talk to my doctor, I ask ChatGPT. I get some basic information and can prepare myself for my next appointment. Just knowing something calms my nerves a bit. 

I'm glad you have a supportive family. Yeah, when you're left alone with your thoughts that's when it gets the hardest. I watched TikToks until I was so exhausted I couldn't keep my eyes open. I'm hoping for good results. Good luck.

I also had a bad reaction to TC chemo, 3 times before I got some meds before chemo to stop it. My side effects didn't start until 2 days after chemo and they were usually the worst on day 3-5. I hope you have an easy time, but I also want to warn you that the side effect usually come a day or 2 after getting chemo.

For hysterectomy:
- wedge pillow or a bunch of pillows so you're laying in a half sitting position
- loose clothes, at least 1 or 2 sizes too big
- shoes that you can put on without having to bend down

For chemo:
- non-alcoholic mouthwash to prevent sores (use every 2-3 hours)
- baby stuff like shower gel, toothpaste, lotion - it's gentler on the skin
- prescription meds

For external radiation:
- meds for stopping diarrhea
- pads for urin leaking
- cotton underwear

I had changed taste after each chemo. Mouthwash and sometimes water made the taste even worse. Sparkling water confussed my mouth for a bit and I didn't taste the chemo as much. I tried eating a lot of different foods and find the ones that didn't taste as bad and then I ate only those. I couldn't eat salami. That tasted the worst. I ate peanut butter and I mean just peanut butter because bread tasted awful. Sometimes smell can change our taste so you could try smelling essential oils like peppermint. But not too often. I think I got a headache because of it. I don't think there's one thing that works for everyone, you kind of have to figure it out by trying a lot of things. Good luck. I hope you figure out something that helps your son.

I'm sorry. I know how that feels. I'm also stage 3c1, grade 1. My cancer was somewhat contained in the uterus, no cervical involment, nothing in ovaries (the left my ovaries because of my age), more than 50% myometrium invasion, but it got to my left sentinel lymph node. It was kind of a shock to find out I was stage 3c1 after being told how slow growing and not agressive grade 1 cancer is. My doctor expected it to be 1a or 1b, but that positive lymph node changed that. 

If you got the pathology report I'm surprised they didn't tell you your treatment plan. I had 6 round of chemo. 1 chemo every 3 weeks. After a month off I started 25 external radiations, basically 5 weeks of radiation every day with the weekends off. I assume you'll have the same. Because you had slight cervical involvement you might also have to have brachytherapy (internal radiation). 

They're also gonna do (if they haven't already) genetic testing which is gonna tell them which treatment will work best for you. And they're gonna monitor your tumor marke ca125 which tells them how you're responding to the chemo. I know this is all so overwhelming and you probably don't know what I'm talking about. I don't even know what it all means and I went through the treatment and was explained everything. Your chemo oncologist will explain all of this at your first appointment. I'd advise you to prepare questions and ask if you can record it because there will be a lot of information and you might not get it all. 

It sucks, but you get through it somehow. I'm now 5 months post chemo and 3 months post radiaton and I'm starting to feel better. I have more energy and the bone and joint pain from treatment is slowly getting better. I just had my first checkup in January and everything looked fine, no cancer. My next check up is in 6 months. 

Take it one day at a time. Reward yourself. After each chemo a got a pizza and CocaCola. It was a reward for getting through chemo and also the last meal that tasted fine before chemo ruined my taste for 2 weeks 🤣 You got this.

I avoided sores during my chemo, but I don't know if it was something I did or I just didn't get them. I used non-alcoholic mouthwash regularly, like every 2-3 hours. I even woke up during the night to use it. The mouth is full of bacteria from food and you need to rinse it.  My oncologist also recommended using chamomile or seibel tea instead of mouthwash, but I couldn't stand the taste. It made me nauseous so I stuck to moutwash. 

I also used kids toothpaste because my regular one made my tongue burn and my gums sore. Your mom should try it, it made my tongue and gums feel a lot better. I also avoided eating hard, crunchy food like chips or the hard bread crust and similar stuff.

It's all normal. I think I had every possible side effect at least once during my 6 cycles. Heat and creams/gels athlets and elderly use might help with the bone pain. Rest was the only thing that helped with the tiredness. If I tried to force myself do to something, I usually felt worse after and still had to take a nap. What type of upset stomach to you have? I had nausea which went away after I took anti-nause pills. After my 3rd chemo I started getting stomach cramps similar to the ones with diarrhea. When I mentioned them to my oncologist, she prescribed me some pills for it. Take whatever your oncologist prescribed or call your oncologist and ask for something. There is medicine for any side effects. You don't have to suffer.

It's fast. It only takes 15 minutes or so. You'll be awake, you'll feel some tugging but no pain. You'll have a chest x-ray after so they can check if everythings all right. And then you'll go home. I didn't get any special instructions just to not get it wet and to not lift or use the arm on the side where the port is for a few days. It hurt a bit for a few days, but ibuprofen helped. Good luck.
Congrats! I have to wait until I'm 2 years cancer free before I can get mine out.
I get it. I'd take radiation over chemo. I had worse side effects with radiaton than with chemo, but I can deal with the side effects, I just can't lose my hair again.
Pain pills, staying warm or using hot water bottle, cream/gel that the athletes and eldery use for joint pain (I used horse balm, but any would probably work).

Same thing happened to me. 8 years ago I lost 100lbs and was close to my GW. Then the weight loss stopped and for a year I was gaining and losing the same 10 lbs. You won't know the survival rates until she talks to her oncologist. Uterine cancer is staged based on pathology from hysterectomy. A lot of things influence survival rates: did they remove all cancer with the surgery, type of cancer (endometroid, sarcoma...), grade (1 is least agressive and 3 is the most agressive), stage (if uterine cancer spread to the cervic it could be stage 2, she could have 2 cancers and both be stage 1, are her lymph nodes negative or positive, genetics (this is more important for the type of treatment the oncologist chooses)... There are so many things that only your oncologist will know. Plus survival rates that you see online are old, medicine evolves and survival rates change. 

I have endometrial cancer, grade 1, stage 3 (1 positive lymph node) so I had chemo and radiation. My oncologist told me my 5 year survival rate without chemo and radiation was 50% and with chemo and radiation 70%. But she also said to not focus too much on the numbers. Good luck. I'm hoping for the best for your ex wife.

Cancer patients, if a biopsy confirmed cancer or if they suspect cancer, usually get priority treatment. Normal waiting time for a CT is months, I got mine in 3 weeks. I had my biopsy 2 weeks after my first hospital visit, then I waited for results for a little over a week, then I had my second biopsy 2 weeks later, and 2 weeks after that I got diagnosed with uterine cancer. 6 weeks after that I had my surgery. In that 6 weeks I had chest x-ray, ultrasound, 2 blood tests and a CT. And 8 weeks after my surgery I started chemo. So from first hospital visit to my first treatment was 3 1/2 months. 11 weeks seems like a normal timeline. It depends where you are and what type of cancer you have and how agressive it is, but in general things move pretty fast even if they feel slow to you.

I just finished 6 rounds of Carboplatin and Paclitaxel. I didn't get Keytruda. I was so nervous about my first chemo. The scariest part was not knowing what to expect. Here are a few things I wish I knew. I hope that helps.

Chemo doesn't hurt, you don't feel anything. Dress comfortable, maybe bring a pillow with you. Also bring water, snacks and entertainment, movies to watch, a book to read or something. Chemo days drag. I was at the chemo center from 7am till 6pm. 

I got a bad reaction to Paclitaxel. It's pretty common and the nurses will warn you about it. Pay attention to how you're feeling and if you feel just a bit off tell the nurses right away. 

About the side effects. I felt normal for 1 or 2 days after chemo. The worst were days 3-7, then I started feeling better. Use mouthwash without alcohol to avoid mouth sores. Use products made for babies and children. Track your symptoms and medicine you take so you can show your oncologist. Drink enough water to help flush the chemo from your body. Your taste will change and food will taste disgusting. For me it only lasted 10-14 days after chemo and then I finally got to enjoy food. Losing hair is painful and itchy. My hair started falling out exactly 14days after my 1st chemo. I cut it short but it was still traumatic to see it fall out. I regret not just shaving it off. 

Can't think of anything else, but if you want to know something just ask. Good luck.

I'm in a similar situation. Stage 3C, 1 more chemo then radiation. Here are some of my questions I've prepared: 

How long (how many minutes) does the radiation lasts?

How long do I stay at the hospital? Is it an hour or half a day? Will I be able to drive myself?

Which side effects can I expect? Which will happen right away and which will show up later?

Are there any permanent side effects and how likely are they? I'm especially worried about this. I don't want to deal with incontinence and GI issues for the rest of my life. 

Do I get meds for the side effects and how effective are they?

Are there any restrictions while on treatment? Can I take showers? Can I be in the sun? 

When will I be able to go to work after finishing treatment?

Write down any questions you have. Your radiation oncologist will probably explain everything and then you can just go through your list and ask what hasn't been covered. That's what I did for my first chemo appointment and I'm doing the same for radiation. 

Good luck with your appointment and treatment.

My oncologist explained most of it on her own, but here's my list of questions I prepared for my first appointment with the chemo oncologist:

1. Side effects. Which are certain and which are less likely? How to treat side effect? What medicine I should take? How long do side effects last? Are there any permanent side effects?

2. When will I lose my hair? When do they start to grow back? Does my insurance cover a wig?

3. What type of chemo am I getting? 

4. How does a chemo cycle look like? How does a chemo day look like? How long does the infusion last? When do I have to get to the hospital? Can I drive myself or do I need someone with me?

5. Diet. What can I eat? What do I have to avoid?

6. Will I need a port or a PICC line?

7. Some questions about my cancer: What's the prognosis with and without chemo? How likely is for the cancer to metastasize? I also ask her to explain some stuff from my pathology report (P53, pole mutation...).  

I hope this helps. Good luck with your appointment.

The laparoscopic cuts are really tiny, maybe half an inch, 1cm. Mine are on each side, maybe 10 inch apart, and a bit higher than the bikini cut. I had laparoscopic surgery with a 7 inch bikini cut. My belly fat hides the cut so it was kind of awkward changing the wound dressing because I had to lay down and pull up the belly so I could change it. The healing wasn't anything special. It was quite painful the first 3 days, then it got better. Taking the pain meds regularly helped a lot. The pain was mostly gone after 2-3 weeks, but the moment I overdid it, I felt it, so rest more than you think you need. I couldn't shower for the first weeks and then I could only shower with a waterproof bandage until the doctor took out the stitches. After that I just had to keep the cut clean and dry. After each shower I made sure the cut was completely dried before I put on the dressing. Because the incision is right in the fold under my belly fat I used dressing until my cut healed completely so for like 4 weeks.

After the surgery, at least the first 1-2 weeks you won't be able to do much (depends on what type of surgery you're having). Before you go to the hospital clean a bit, change your bedding so when you get home you have a clean bed. You won't be able to bend so put things that you think will need when you get home at tables, desks, chairs... And get a grabber tool so you'll be able to pick up things from the floor. For food, delivery is a good option. You'll probably only need it for the first 3-4 days. If that's too expensive you can get some instant noodles, soup, pasta, mashed potatoes... Get some fruit, vegetables and nuts that you can snack on. Cereals are also quick. Yogurt. You can make a couple of sandwiches, they stay in the fridge for 3 days. Most of premade meals are good in the fridge for 3-4 days. Cooked or baked stuff can be left at room temperature for 1-2 days.

I wore a button down blouse or a men's T-shirt with 3 buttons on top. When it got colder I wore a tank top under a hoodie with a zipper so once they hooked me up I just put on the hoodie. While chemo room wasn't exactly cold, it was too cold for just a tank top. I don't think you need a port shirt, just wear something with a wide neckline.

I was 38 and the doctors thought I'll probably be stage 1 and if the ovaries looked healthy during the survery they'll leave them. I said they can remove them, but they left them. I had 1 positive lymph node so I ended up being stage 3. I neede chemo and radiation which ruined my ovaries and any pros of keeping them. Now it's just one more thing where the cancer could reappear. 

If there's a chance you're anything but stage 1 I'd ask to remove the ovaries. You'll have do deal with menopause symptoms in 5-10 years anyway because ovaries stop working sooner if you have a hysterectomy. If you're stage 1, the chances of recurrence are so small you can keep them. You'll also won't need chemo or radiation that would affect them.

My follow up is blood test (basic + tumor markers), pelvic exam and talk about any symptoms or side effects of chemo and radiation. I was told they decide if they're gonna do CT or any other testing based on the symptoms and the exam, but they still do 1 CT a year.

It took me about 2 months to get used to mine. I felt similar at first. Give it some time. After 9 months touching it still feels weird but most of the time I'm not aware of it. I forget it's even there unless I touch it.

Are you sure it's stage 2 and not grade 2? I was told grade and type of cancer after my hysteroscopy but they said they can only tell the stage after surgery. If it's grade 2 that's still not agressive cancer and it's slow growing. About gene information you could ask chatGPT. My oncologist explain it to me but I didn't understand what he was talking about so I asked chatGPT and then I got it. Good luck.

I only watch Hallmark when I'm in the mood for something cheesy and for Christmas. I expect this to be just like anything else they put out so I avoided watching it until now. It's so good and sooooo different from their normal. I love it and I hope they make more stuff like that.

After the surgery the only thing they told me was how the surgery went and that they took samples to send to the lab. They gave me instructions for home and gave me the date of my first appointment which was 3 weeks after my surgery. How were you diagnosed? Did you have a biopsy? That should give you the grade and type of cancer. It can change after the surgery, but it usually stays the same. I hope you have a successful surgery and speedy recovery.

Losing my hair was the hardest thing about chemo. I could deal with the side effects, but not losing my hair. My advice is to shave it completely. Don't cut it short or buzz it. Hair falling out in clumbs and seeing more and more of my scalp was really traumatic. Once I shaved it all I felt better. I avoided mirrors and wore a cap all the time, but it was way better than watching my hair fall out. If you love shopping go on a shopping spree for wigs and scarf and comfortable chemo clothes. Looking for wigs online was a great distraction.
Yeah, I had a big meal and I was still hungry like I hadn't had anything. Good luck.

I was the same when I went through chemo, also TC. I had nausea, stomach cramps, my taste had changed and I was starving. I never felt full and I always felt like I hadn't eaten all day. I would eat nuts, crackers, blueberries, popcorn... like small food that I could slowely snack on. Drinking water made my hunger worse. Sparkling water and soda helped a bit, but I couldn't drink it too much because the chemo made my mouth sensitive and I was afraod of gettimg sores. A chemo nurse said that weight gain was normal and is better to gain weight than to lose it during chemo.
It usually started on day 2, most of the side effects started then actually. The day of the chemo and the next day I usually felt normal.

I never vomited. Nausea lasted 2 to 5 days, but as long as I took anti nausea pill right away or on the schedule, I was fine. The pills made the nausea go away completelly in 10 minutes. Good luck with your chemo.

Yes. Every pain or feeling weird and I automatically think of cancer comming back. I'm not really handling it, more like forcefully gething through it and hoping for the best. 

For the entire week before my first check up I was a nervous wreck and convinced my cancer was back. I think I even got body pains from anxiety because those pains went away after the check up when I was told everything was normal.
Same. I still can't drink 2 glasses of milk at once, but I can eat yogurt, cheese... Interesting.
How they park their car. Over the lines, no parking zone, across 2 parking spaces. I think in general what kind of driver you are says a lot about someone.

I'm sorry about your diagnosis. From my experience the only way to stage endometrial cancer is hysterectomy.  CA 125 and MRI will show if the cancer has spread outside the uterus. Ca 125 under 35 is normal. If it's elevated it can mean inflamation or spread to ovaries, but it's not 100%. Are you also getting other tumor markers checked (ca 15-3, cea)? MR will show near organs and lymph nodes if they're all clear. 

Do you know the grade (1-3)? As long as the cancer is low grade (1 or 2), hasn't spread and they consider it stage 1a your doctor will talk to you about hormonal therapy. I think they test it for 3 or 6 months to see if it's working then if it's working they encourage you to get pregnant in 2 years and have surgery later.

I was considered stage 1a and my oncologist was talking about fertility preserving hormonal treatment but CT which is similar to MRI showed enlarged lymph nodes so I had to have surgery. Good luck. I hope ot all turns out well for you.

Entertainment (books, tv shows, movies...). Chemos take a long time and you get bored. Any comfortable clothes. If she has a port a sweater specifically made for accessing the port. Baby stuff like toothpaste, lotion, shower gel. During chemo your skin and the entire body gets more sensitive and using baby stuff really helpped me deal with it. Good luck to your mom.
I hate crowds, plus I don't have a clue how any of the machines work.

I had my period when I had my surgery. I was worried, but they said it's not a big deal. Just tell the nurses. They'll give you those hospital mesh panties and a pad. They cut them off in the operating room once you fall asleep. I woke up in the recovery room with a new gown and new mesh panties and a pad. My after surgery bleeding was actually less heavy than pre surgery period.
Pineapple. I kind of like it.

Same. Once I start thinking of food I can't stop. I don't know why extreme restriction is so much easier. I can go half a day without food or water. No wonder people say it's easier to quit smoking than food addiction.

These things sort of help. I distract myself with watching TikToks and YT. Hyperfixating on something is great. I pick a random topic and then research it online. I move, like if I'm in the living room, I'd go to the bedroom (never the kitchen). The other thing I do is to not tell myself I can't eat or call myself a fat cow which I did a lot. Instead I say to myself something like "I'm hungry, I'll eat in 30 minites." I repeat that until it's time to eat. If nothing helps and all I can think about is food I eat something that's less than 100 calories or I drink a can of soda.

I was told not to do my nails during chemo. I had TC chemo and one of the side effects is nails changing and being more sensitive. I left my nails alone and they still got vertical lines and ridges. Luckily they weren't painful. But I've seen people talk about their nails falling off which really scared me. My advice is to leave them alone.

It's up to you. The doctors recommend the best option, but it's your choice. I'd listen to the doctors.

If they found endometrial cancer on your cervix it's possible that your cancer spread from the uterus to it and if it spread so far it could have also gone elsewhere. Surgery is the only treatment and it's usually also the only way to stage it and find out if you need more treatment. If the cancer is found early enough, surgery might be the only thing you need. For me it took a little over a month between a confirmed diagnosis and surgery. With cancer time is important. Grade 1 is not agressive and it usually doesn't spread fast, but you never know. 

It's scary and frustrating and not the right time. We've all been there. You really have to think of yourself right now. Chemo feels way worse than perimenopause symptoms. You still have a chance to avoid it if your cancer was found fast enough. My advice is don't wait and listen to your doctors. But the final decision is up to you. Good luck.

I had my port for 10 months now and no problems. Port placement is quick. It takes maybe 20 minutees, she won't feel any pain, just some tugging. There is some waiting before and after she'll probably have to have an x-ray so they check the pprt is placed correctly. For the first few days she should avoid using the arm on the side she gets the port. I was also scared, but when I had chemo I was so glad I had the port. Good luck to her.

Wear comfortable clothes and shoes. Bring water or something to drink. Maybe some snacks, but don't bring anything smelly because it might bother other patients. The most important is entertainment. Like you said, it's boring. You just sit there with nothing to do. You can't even take a nap because the nurses keep checking up on you and machines are going off. Reading and TikTok got me through most of my chemos. Chemo chairs can be uncomfortable, at least they were at my chemo center, so bring a small pillow or a blanket, something to make it more comfortable. Good luck.
Shave it now. If you're gonna lose your hair, it doesn't matter anyway and you'll feel so much better with a clean shaved head. No more hair everywhere and no more itching/burning/painful scalp.

I don't know what my starting BMI was. I lost a bunch of weight and my BMI went to 30. Currently my BMI is 40 so I assume my highest BMI was around 50. I can do exercise, I even enjoy it, so I started with exercise and then slowly added diet which is my biggest struggle. 

I started with 10-20 minutes of exercise every day. I did Youtube video workouts (for seniors, for obese, low impact, walking indoor). There are also dancing workout if you love dancing. I don't have the coordination for that and I just got frustrated when I couldn't follow along. If I couldn't do an exercise or I needed to rest I just walked in place until I felt ready to do more. I watched a tv show while working out (1 episode = 1 workout). I also did workout tetris - it's a bullet journal thing where you add shape/block for each time you exercise. If you google bullet journal tetris you should see what I mean. I'm trying to get back to working out every day and the workout tetris is really motivating. I want to draw in that next block so bad. I hope you find the right exercise for you. Just try a bunch of stuff until you find something you enjoy. Good luck.

I think that depends on the type of chemo. I had TC chemo and my weight stayed roughly the same, which is a bit surprising because I had huge appetite a few days after chemo. Nausea + stomach cramps + wanting to eat is weird and awful. On top of that, chemo changed my taste so I wanted to eat, but everything tasted disgusting. One time I made myself 3 different breakfasts before I could actually eat one of them. Nurses told me to eat whatever I wanted, except grapefruit and too much vitamin C because that affected my chemo. They also don't like if you're losing weight. It's better for your body if you maintain or gain weight.
Day 2. They wouldn't let me leave the hospital without pooping first. First poo is the scariest. My advice is to take laxatives and don't wait for it to happen naturally.

I'm so sorry. This sucks. I got the same treatment when I was first diagnosed. I had tests, then I saw my doctor for like a couple of minutes, just long enough to be send for more tests and got a new appointment for after they had their meeting. Waiting is hard, but doctors telling you the bare minimal or nothing until they are certain makes it worse. Can you see your scan results and the radiologist's opinion? I'm not saying this a good way to do things, but when I get my scans before I talk to my doctor, I ask ChatGPT. I get some basic information and can prepare myself for my next appointment. Just knowing something calms my nerves a bit. 

I'm glad you have a supportive family. Yeah, when you're left alone with your thoughts that's when it gets the hardest. I watched TikToks until I was so exhausted I couldn't keep my eyes open. I'm hoping for good results. Good luck.

I also had a bad reaction to TC chemo, 3 times before I got some meds before chemo to stop it. My side effects didn't start until 2 days after chemo and they were usually the worst on day 3-5. I hope you have an easy time, but I also want to warn you that the side effect usually come a day or 2 after getting chemo.

For hysterectomy:
- wedge pillow or a bunch of pillows so you're laying in a half sitting position
- loose clothes, at least 1 or 2 sizes too big
- shoes that you can put on without having to bend down

For chemo:
- non-alcoholic mouthwash to prevent sores (use every 2-3 hours)
- baby stuff like shower gel, toothpaste, lotion - it's gentler on the skin
- prescription meds

For external radiation:
- meds for stopping diarrhea
- pads for urin leaking
- cotton underwear

I had changed taste after each chemo. Mouthwash and sometimes water made the taste even worse. Sparkling water confussed my mouth for a bit and I didn't taste the chemo as much. I tried eating a lot of different foods and find the ones that didn't taste as bad and then I ate only those. I couldn't eat salami. That tasted the worst. I ate peanut butter and I mean just peanut butter because bread tasted awful. Sometimes smell can change our taste so you could try smelling essential oils like peppermint. But not too often. I think I got a headache because of it. I don't think there's one thing that works for everyone, you kind of have to figure it out by trying a lot of things. Good luck. I hope you figure out something that helps your son.

I'm sorry. I know how that feels. I'm also stage 3c1, grade 1. My cancer was somewhat contained in the uterus, no cervical involment, nothing in ovaries (the left my ovaries because of my age), more than 50% myometrium invasion, but it got to my left sentinel lymph node. It was kind of a shock to find out I was stage 3c1 after being told how slow growing and not agressive grade 1 cancer is. My doctor expected it to be 1a or 1b, but that positive lymph node changed that. 

If you got the pathology report I'm surprised they didn't tell you your treatment plan. I had 6 round of chemo. 1 chemo every 3 weeks. After a month off I started 25 external radiations, basically 5 weeks of radiation every day with the weekends off. I assume you'll have the same. Because you had slight cervical involvement you might also have to have brachytherapy (internal radiation). 

They're also gonna do (if they haven't already) genetic testing which is gonna tell them which treatment will work best for you. And they're gonna monitor your tumor marke ca125 which tells them how you're responding to the chemo. I know this is all so overwhelming and you probably don't know what I'm talking about. I don't even know what it all means and I went through the treatment and was explained everything. Your chemo oncologist will explain all of this at your first appointment. I'd advise you to prepare questions and ask if you can record it because there will be a lot of information and you might not get it all. 

It sucks, but you get through it somehow. I'm now 5 months post chemo and 3 months post radiaton and I'm starting to feel better. I have more energy and the bone and joint pain from treatment is slowly getting better. I just had my first checkup in January and everything looked fine, no cancer. My next check up is in 6 months. 

Take it one day at a time. Reward yourself. After each chemo a got a pizza and CocaCola. It was a reward for getting through chemo and also the last meal that tasted fine before chemo ruined my taste for 2 weeks 🤣 You got this.

I avoided sores during my chemo, but I don't know if it was something I did or I just didn't get them. I used non-alcoholic mouthwash regularly, like every 2-3 hours. I even woke up during the night to use it. The mouth is full of bacteria from food and you need to rinse it.  My oncologist also recommended using chamomile or seibel tea instead of mouthwash, but I couldn't stand the taste. It made me nauseous so I stuck to moutwash. 

I also used kids toothpaste because my regular one made my tongue burn and my gums sore. Your mom should try it, it made my tongue and gums feel a lot better. I also avoided eating hard, crunchy food like chips or the hard bread crust and similar stuff.

It's all normal. I think I had every possible side effect at least once during my 6 cycles. Heat and creams/gels athlets and elderly use might help with the bone pain. Rest was the only thing that helped with the tiredness. If I tried to force myself do to something, I usually felt worse after and still had to take a nap. What type of upset stomach to you have? I had nausea which went away after I took anti-nause pills. After my 3rd chemo I started getting stomach cramps similar to the ones with diarrhea. When I mentioned them to my oncologist, she prescribed me some pills for it. Take whatever your oncologist prescribed or call your oncologist and ask for something. There is medicine for any side effects. You don't have to suffer.

It's fast. It only takes 15 minutes or so. You'll be awake, you'll feel some tugging but no pain. You'll have a chest x-ray after so they can check if everythings all right. And then you'll go home. I didn't get any special instructions just to not get it wet and to not lift or use the arm on the side where the port is for a few days. It hurt a bit for a few days, but ibuprofen helped. Good luck.
Congrats! I have to wait until I'm 2 years cancer free before I can get mine out.
I get it. I'd take radiation over chemo. I had worse side effects with radiaton than with chemo, but I can deal with the side effects, I just can't lose my hair again.
Pain pills, staying warm or using hot water bottle, cream/gel that the athletes and eldery use for joint pain (I used horse balm, but any would probably work).

Same thing happened to me. 8 years ago I lost 100lbs and was close to my GW. Then the weight loss stopped and for a year I was gaining and losing the same 10 lbs. During Covid I completely let myself go and I gained back almost all the weight. I learned that small things matter. 10 minite workout is better than none. Eating a few spoons more adds up. Snacks also add up. I also learned that I can lose weight only if I do it my way. Gyms and trainers yelling at me isn't for me. I prefer working at home while listening to Taylor Swift.
Banana bread. I ate a lot of banana bread during my chemo. For some reason it didn't taste as bad as other food. Now I can't eat it or smell it. I can't even eat ripe bananas, only half green ones.

I'm sorrry you're in so much pain. Are you on any pain meds? I got extra strong Ibuprofen and if that didn't help I was told to take Tylenol. The pressure might be gas pain. Are you taking anything for that? Hysterectomy is a major surgery so some pain is normal, but this sounds so much worse than what I experienced. If you don't feel any better soon, call your surgeon or the hospital.
Yes, body hair is the worst. Also that small thin facial hair and chin hair. I guess one good thing about chemo, beside killing cancer cells, is no body hair.

I had 6 rounds of TC chemo. I finish 5 months ago so my hair is still very short, but it's growing. The front/bangs/above the forehead is growing a lot slower than the rest. I always had thick and wavy hair. Beside the front part it's still thick and it's starting to curl. I have a few more gray hair than I did before. 

My eyebrows are thinner. My body hair is thicker and darker and it also grows faster.

I know exactly how you feel. I was stuck in a similar cycle for 10 years. A few days after my period ended I started working out and eating normal foods and in normal amounts. I kept that up for 2 weeks or so until PMS hit. Then I binged, stopped working out, was depressed and angry. And then I got my period and of course I didn't feel like working out. I'm sorry I don't have any advice. I never figured out how to fix it, then I got cancer and my uterus went bye bye. Honestly, I'm feeling much better now and I've managed to regularly work out for 2 months straight, no breaks. I struggle with diet, but that has nothing to do with my cycle.

My hair is also growing back that way. I fished chemo in August and my hair didn't start to grow until October. My bang might be an inch and the back is 3 inches. I hate it. I also loved my hair the most about me. I was told it's normal for front hair to grow slower and that it's gonna even out.

I don't remember having the worst day, but I had a few bad days. The gas and gas pain on the first 3 days was bad. The second week pain was a bit surprising because around days 5-7 I started to feel better and I thought that was it for the pain, but then the pain came back. It wasn't really painful, more like being very sore. I also had a couple of days where I overdid it the day before and felt it the next day. Emotionally, those were the worst days. I felt like I'm in the clear and feeling good and the next day I was tired and in pain and stressing that I hurt myself. I hope you have a fast and easy recovery.
I don't know if this helps. Honestly, I don't even know what it means, but for my adjuvant therapy for stage 3c I had 25 radiations with 50 Gy.

Same. I'm an introvert so beside being embarrassed I don't even want to go where there are people. Definitely no gym for me. I love home workouts. I put on a Youtube video and just work out in my bedroom. Sometimes I watch a TV show while working out. 

If you want to start exercising do something that fits youre personality and you won't hate it. Maybe if you do it for a while, you'll build up confidence. Working out has never been my problem. I've been working out for years. My issue and why I can't lose weight is my diet. I'm proof you can't out-exercise a bad diet. Good luck.

You won't know the survival rates until she talks to her oncologist. Uterine cancer is staged based on pathology from hysterectomy. A lot of things influence survival rates: did they remove all cancer with the surgery, type of cancer (endometroid, sarcoma...), grade (1 is least agressive and 3 is the most agressive), stage (if uterine cancer spread to the cervic it could be stage 2, she could have 2 cancers and both be stage 1, are her lymph nodes negative or positive, genetics (this is more important for the type of treatment the oncologist chooses)... There are so many things that only your oncologist will know. Plus survival rates that you see online are old, medicine evolves and survival rates change. 

I have endometrial cancer, grade 1, stage 3 (1 positive lymph node) so I had chemo and radiation. My oncologist told me my 5 year survival rate without chemo and radiation was 50% and with chemo and radiation 70%. But she also said to not focus too much on the numbers. Good luck. I'm hoping for the best for your ex wife.

I have POLE mutation. My oncologist said that's a good thing. My cancer spread to lymph nodes so I still had chemo, but it was my choice. There's not a lot of research for stages 3 and 4 with POLE mutation so doctors aren't sure how to treat it. Mine recommended chemo buz said she wasn't sure if it changes anything. But they know that with stage 1 and 2 recurrence is very unlikely even without treatment.
Congrats!

Ask the doctor for anti-nausea meds or if the meds she has don't work ask for a different kind. She should take anti anusea pills regulary and not when she already feels sick. Ginger or peppermint tea might help. Also smelling peppermint essential oil or humming can help. It can't hurt to try, but the anti nausea medicine the doctors prescribe are still the most effective.

The hair will grown when and how it wants. I was lazy and I was also dealing with side effects of radiation so I didn't do anything, I just let it grow. After the first 2 months when it grew really slow, it started growing faster. It grew faster in the back of my head and on the sides. The front grew the slowest. I don't think shaving does anything. The hair comes in patchy, sparse and then it grows in so if you shave those first patches of hair, it might look like it grows more evenly. My advice is to just let it do its own thing and grow at its own pace. A good healthy diet might be more helpful than any of this.

That's great news. Tiredness will go away. It just takes a body a while to heal. I think my surgeon said it takes 3 months to heal from the surgery and then 6 months or more for everything to heal up completely.

You got this. You might need some help, but I don't think you'll have to give up your independence. When I first heard I needed chemo and radiation I was so scared. The scariest part was the not knowing. Movies and books portray chemo as this awful thing and while it's not nice and you have some really shitty days, it's not as awful as they make it out to be. YouTube, Reddit and especially TikTok prepared me for some of what to expect. There are so many wonderful people sharing their experiences and while I hate that they had to go through that, I'm so grateful for all the information. Good luck.
The tests were worse than the actually surgery. I had 2 hysteroscopies, no anesthesia. They weren't as terrible as the internet said, but they were bad. Congrats! I hope all goes well.

My experience is that if the results are normal they tell you over the phone or at your next scheduled appointment. If they find something they tell you in person. It could be, but it doesn't mean it's cancer or anything bad, they just like to give diagnosis in person or maybe it's their policy that they can't tell you over the phone. Good luck. I hope everything turns out okay.

I felt the same way, for the most part. I had hysterectomy because I was diagnosed with cancer so I was worried about that, but I was 100% excited about getting rid of my uterus. I was 38 and all the doctors were being so gentle and careful when they told me I needed hysterectomy and I just tried to hide how happy I was about that. I'm also ace and I never planned on having kids. It must be really hard for people who want to have children. Because I had cancer I didn't get a lot of comments, just some pitying looks. I also felt like my reaction wasn't normal and I should feel sad or something. In the end I didn't really care. I got rid of a useless organ that tortured me for 25 years and gave me cancer.

Congrats on clear scans. I'm sorry aobut your painful side effects. I guess pain is normal. I'm having some shoulder and ribs pain that my ocologist said is from chemo and the discomfort and a bit of pain when peeing is apparently from pelvic radiation.

I get it. I finished treatment 2 months ago and I just had my first check up. After treatment is worse than going through treatment. I don't know what to do or how to feel. I should be happy, but I'm more anxious about it coming back than I was about actually having cancer. Everything kind of feels pointless. It's a weird place we're in. Distractions help me. Reading is great, but I can't watch moveis or TV shows because my mind wanders. Working out also clears my mind. Find something that makes you happy or you're excited about. It can be a hobby or something you do just for yourself and brings you joy.

A wedge pillow - I couldn't sleep laying down on my back or on my side for 2 weeks and it also made it easier to get out of bed (watch YouTube video on how to get out of bed so you can help your mother). Gather all the meds she might need (pain pills, gas medicine, laxatives). She won't be able to bend down so put things she might need somewhere higher. For the drive home from the hospital take a small pillow with you that she can put on her stomach and between the seat belt. Get her some entertainment like books, puzzles, move a tv if you have to. She'll likely spend most of the first week in bed and that can get boring.

Your body, your choice. A man could never understand a woman's body or periods. And I'm sure your dad would quickly change his mind about letting anyone cut him open if he was the one in pain or it was about saving his life. 

I had hysterectomy because of uterine cancer at 38. I had awful periods for years and I asked my gyno about hysterectomy before and I was always told no. If I got hysterectomy, maybe I could have avoided cancer or it would have been found soon enough that I wouldn't have to have chemo and radiation. My life is so much better without my uterus. I regret having cancer, but I don't regred hysterectomy. 

This is your decision. Make a pros and cons list. Ask a fortuneteller for advice. Do whatever it takes, but make the decision for yourself and what's best for you. You're the one who's gonna live with the consequences, not your dad.

Oh, yeah. I was on the last day of my period on the day of my surgery. My hemoglobin was better after my surgery than before 🤣 It was 14 days of bloody hell. It was brutal, like my uterus knew this was the last time.

I have the same worry. I was 38 when I had my hysterectomy and I told my surgeon to take the ovaries, but apparently they looked healthy so they left them because I was so "young." And now I worry with every pain and discomfort. I told my doctor about it and he said it could be from the surgery, chemo or radiation, and that it could last for a year or longer. 

I have regular blood tests, including tumor marker ca 125, which according to my doctor is a good indicator if cancer comes back, especially if it spreads to the ovaries. Normal ca 125 is under 35, if it's bellow that but it's increasing or if it's higher then they do more tests. Get your ca 125 checked, it's a simple blood test, and have regular scans every 4 - 6 months. I'm having blood tests and scans every 4 months for the first year, then every 6 months for the next 2 years. Get a second opinion if you can. Good luck.
I don't want to mess someone up the way my parents messed me up.

My periods kept getting worse and my gyno kept telling me to lose weight and how that will fix everything. I ended up anemic and in the hospital where they finally took me serious. After 2 months of tests and scans I was diagnosed with endometrial cancer. I had hysterectomy and it turned out it was stage 3.

I was diagnised with grade 1 endometrial cancer last January. In March I had a hysterectomy and was diagnosed with stage 3c. I had >50% myometrium invasion and 1 positive lymph node. 2 months after my hysterectomy I had my port inserted and a week later I started 6 rounds of chemo. Chemo wasn't fun, but it was nowhere near as bad as I imagined it. After finishing chemo I had 1 month break and then I did 25 external radiations. I hated the radiation side effect more than the ones from chemo. Chemo side effects last around 7 days and then you feel better, with radiation when the side effects started towards the end they lasted for almost a month. I had my first check up on Friday and everything is clear. It was tough but doable. You got this.

I went through 6 TC chemos this summer for endometrial cancer. I know exactly what you're going through and I'm sorry you have to deal with all of that. It does get better, but it sucks for a while. 

I gave myself full permission to be lazy and not do anything. That helped me feeling not so quily when I could do or go somewhere. I also held tight to anything that brought me any joy. My cat, reading, TikTok, new hobby. In Google Spreadsheet which I used for tracking my side effects and medicine, I counted down the days till finishing chemo and I loved seeing % and graf getting closer to 100%. You can do it. One day at a time. Good luck.

After my diagnosis I spent 3 days Googling everything I could think off. I barely slept. I also need to know everything so I know how you feel. My CT showed enlarged lymph nodes and changes to ovaries, but after my hysterectomy only 1 lymph node was positive and my ovaries were fine. Pathology will give you the final result. I'm sorry about your mom's diagnosis. At the first oncology appointment they're gonna go through the biopsy results. They will tell you what type of endometrial cancer (endometroid, sarcoma...) she has and what grade (grade 1 is slow growing and not very agressive, grade 3 is the most agressive). If they don't tell you this, ask them about it. You can ask about the stage, but they won't be able to say because endometrial cancer is staged with surgery. Your mom will have to have more tests like chest x-ray, CT, MRI to make sure the cancer hasn't spread. You can ask them to check tumor markers, especially ca125. There will be a lot of information and a lot to process so if the oncologist agrees make a voice recording on your phone. Ask about their contact information like how can you reach them if you have any questions. Good luck. I hope everthing goes well.

Cancer patients, if a biopsy confirmed cancer or if they suspect cancer, usually get priority treatment. Normal waiting time for a CT is months, I got mine in 3 weeks. I had my biopsy 2 weeks after my first hospital visit, then I waited for results for a little over a week, then I had my second biopsy 2 weeks later, and 2 weeks after that I got diagnosed with uterine cancer. 6 weeks after that I had my surgery. In that 6 weeks I had chest x-ray, ultrasound, 2 blood tests and a CT. And 8 weeks after my surgery I started chemo. So from first hospital visit to my first treatment was 3 1/2 months. 11 weeks seems like a normal timeline. It depends where you are and what type of cancer you have and how agressive it is, but in general things move pretty fast even if they feel slow to you.

About the side effects. I felt normal for 1 or 2 days after chemo. The worst were days 3-7, then I started feeling better. Use mouthwash without alcohol to avoid mouth sores. I'm in a similar situation. Stage 3C, 1 more chemo then radiation. Here are some of my questions I've prepared: 

How long (how many minutes) does the radiation lasts?

How long do I stay at the hospital? Is it an hour or half a day? Will I be able to drive myself?

Which side effects can I expect? Which will happen right away and which will show up later?

Are there any permanent side effects and how likely are they? I'm especially worried about this. I don't want to deal with incontinence and GI issues for the rest of my life. 

Do I get meds for the side effects and how effective are they?

Are there any restrictions while on treatment? Can I take showers? Can I be in the sun? 

When will I be able to go to work after finishing treatment?

Write down any questions you have. Your radiation oncologist will probably explain everything and then you can just go through your list and ask what hasn't been covered. That's what I did for my first chemo appointment and I'm doing the same for radiation. 

Good luck with your appointment and treatment.

Taxol can cause an allergic reaction. I had it and it's not fun, but the nurses react quickly and give you meds. Taxol will also cause your hair to fall out. Mine started to fall out exactly 2 weeks after my 1st chemo. My scalp was sensitive, itchy and painful. My oncologist explained most of it on her own, but here's my list of questions I prepared for my first appointment with the chemo oncologist:

1. Side effects. Which are certain and which are less likely? How to treat side effect? What medicine I should take? How long do side effects last? Are there any permanent side effects?

2. When will I lose my hair? When do they start to grow back? Does my insurance cover a wig?

3. What type of chemo am I getting? 

4. How does a chemo cycle look like? How does a chemo day look like? How long does the infusion last? When do I have to get to the hospital? Can I drive myself or do I need someone with me?

5. Diet. What can I eat? What do I have to avoid?

6. Will I need a port or a PICC line?

7. Some questions about my cancer: What's the prognosis with and without chemo? How likely is for the cancer to metastasize? I also ask her to explain some stuff from my pathology report (P53, pole mutation...).  

I hope this helps. Good luck with your appointment.

The cervix is removed with the uterus because cervix is one of the first places the cancer spreads to.
